title: Why a flat SIP isn't enough
objectives: Explain inflation erosion in rupee terms.
Explain how income growth and compounding both favour a step-up.
body_md:
A flat SIP is a decision that gets quietly worse every year.

## Inflation erodes it

At 6% inflation, ₹10,000 a month in 20 years buys only what about ₹3,100 buys today. The instalment stays the same in rupees and shrinks in what it can buy.

## Income usually grows

A SIP that stays flat becomes a smaller share of income every year. A client who started at 15% of income may be at 6% a decade later, without ever deciding to save less.

## Compounding rewards it

Later, bigger instalments still have years to grow, so a step-up adds more than its rupee value suggests. That is why a 10% step-up can roughly double a long-term outcome.

## The honest side

A step-up invests far more in total, so it only works if income grows too. Show the total invested beside the final value, every time.
example: A client's ₹10,000 SIP was 15% of take-home pay in 2015. After three increments it is 7% of a larger salary, and the family's spending has absorbed the rest — lifestyle creep, not a decision.
say: Inflation means the same instalment buys less every year.
A flat SIP quietly becomes a smaller share of your income.
never: Your SIP is fine as it is; inflation is only 6%.
The step-up will double your money.

talk_track.title: Why a flat SIP isn't enough
talk_track.text: Why isn't a flat SIP enough? Three reasons. First, inflation erodes it. At six percent inflation, ten thousand rupees a month in twenty years buys only what about three thousand one hundred buys today. Second, income usually grows, so a SIP that stays flat becomes a smaller and smaller share of income each year. And third, compounding rewards stepping up: the later, bigger instalments still have years to grow.

check.q: What step-up rate is usually comfortable?
o: At or below expected income growth, often 5–10%
Above income growth, to catch up
check.why: At or below expected income growth. A step-up faster than income growth squeezes the budget within a few years.

check.q: How does a flat SIP behave as income grows?
o: It becomes a smaller share of income every year
It stays the same share of income
check.why: The rupee amount is flat while income rises, so the saving rate quietly falls.

check.q: What must be shown alongside the final value of a step-up illustration?
o: The total amount invested, which is also much higher
check.why: A step-up invests far more in total. Showing only the result hides the extra money the client has to find.
